cues.text: In 1948, a devout person donated a life-size statue of the Sacred Heart of Jesus to the monastery church of Rosano, near Florence, Italy, fulfilling a promise made during the dangers of the Second World War.
The statue, showing the Heart at the center of Christ's chest surrounded by a crown of thorns, took its place in the church without any expectation of what would follow.
On the evening of April 4, 1948, during the chanting of Vespers, those present noticed for the first time what appeared to be drops of blood falling from the statue's eyes.

Roughly two months later, in June, a further phenomenon began: blood appeared to flow from the statue itself, an event that would recur intermittently over the following two years, witnessed repeatedly by the resident nuns and by numerous visitors.

The monastery preserved sworn testimonies from priests, preachers, and visitors who witnessed the events between 1948 and 1950, along with medical analyses of the substance and cloths used to absorb it, all kept in the monastery archives.
Among the witnesses was Benedetto Tenaci, abbot of Bagno, who recorded seeing the statue bleed from the left arm on May 20, 1948.

On November 14, 1950, by order of the Holy Office, the statue was removed from public view and kept in a safe location — a directive that stands in contrast to the formal approvals other twentieth-century Eucharistic and devotional accounts.
Rosano's account differs from most others in this exhibition because its central object was a devotional statue rather than a consecrated Host.
The Church's own recorded response was to withdraw it from public veneration rather than approve it.

What survives is a well-documented local memory — dated testimonies, preserved samples, a statue's history from a wartime promise to a directive of removal — offered here as inherited devotional record rather than a settled or endorsed sign.
